top3.title: Daughters of the Dust—with Ashley Clark
top3.why: Film critic and curator Ashley Clark discusses and signs his book on Julie Dash's Daughters of the Dust, the landmark 1991 Gullah-set indie drama — a rare chance at real critical context on an underseen American classic, hosted at a brewery rather than a lecture hall. No cost listed.

top3.title: 🚧 Make Your First Website
top3.venue: Iffy Books, 404 S. 20th St., Philadelphia, 19146, United States
top3.why: Iffy Books runs its own HTML-from-scratch workshop, teaching the basics of building and hosting a static personal site on Neocities — reclaiming the web from platforms, one page at a time. Led by Ragman/Richard Green; no experience needed, laptops optional. Pay-what-you-can, suggested $10–$25, nobody turned away for lack of funds.

top3.title: SUBURBAN SASQUATCH (2004)
top3.why: A gloriously dumb double feature of DIY backyard-budget monster movies — 2004's Suburban Sasquatch and 2016's Bigfoot Runs Amok — screened the communal, so-bad-it's-good way PhilaMOCA does best. Doors at 7:00, screening at 7:30. $12 for both films.

top3.title: Demographic Anxieties: A Conversation with Gala Rexer
top3.venue: Wooden Shoe Books, 704 South St, Philadelphia, PA 19147
top3.why: Gala Rexer (University of Warwick) and Nada Matta (Drexel) discuss Rexer's new book on how Israeli state surveillance and border policy shape Palestinian women's reproductive freedom, drawn from two years of ethnographic fieldwork. Dense, serious political-education programming — exactly what Wooden Shoe anchors. Free.

top3.title: Eugene Debs: American Socialist
top3.why: A talk tied to a new book on Eugene Debs — five-time Socialist Party presidential candidate and the most prominent socialist in American history. Rare to see an event built explicitly around Debs rather than invoking him in passing; useful grounding for anyone interested in the real history behind 'democratic socialism.' Free, Rittenhouse Square.

top3.title: Chat Pile
top3.why: Chat Pile's lurching sludge-noise headlines over Philly's own Soul Glo, whose ferocious, explicitly political hardcore has made them one of the most vital bands the city's produced this decade. Shallowater and Skullpresser round out a stacked bill.
